candidate.answerReason: The integer cost equation has the unique positive solution N = 11, B = 2, J = 3. The jam therefore costs 165 cents.

methods.label: Factor the total cost
methods.explanation:
Work in cents so that all quantities are integers. Each sandwich costs \(4B+5J\) cents, giving
\[
N(4B+5J)=253=11\cdot23.
\]
Since \(11\) and \(23\) are prime, the positive divisors of \(253\) are \(1,11,23,253\). We know \(N>1\), and \(B,J\ge1\) makes each sandwich cost at least \(9\) cents. These conditions leave only \(N=11\) or \(N=23\).

If \(N=23\), then \(4B+5J=11\). Positivity forces \(J=1\), but that leaves \(4B=6\), impossible for an integer \(B\).

If \(N=11\), then \(4B+5J=23\). Since \(4B\ge4\), we have \(5J\le19\), so \(J\) is \(1,2\), or \(3\). The corresponding values of \(4B\) are \(18,13\), and \(8\). Only \(8\) is divisible by \(4\), giving \(B=2\) and \(J=3\).

These exhaust the possible sandwich counts and ingredient amounts. The total jam cost is
\[
5NJ=5\cdot11\cdot3=165\text{ cents},
\]
or \(\boxed{\$1.65}\), choice (D).
methods.levelReason: Small-number factorization and a bounded search for positive integer solutions suffice; formal congruence machinery is unnecessary.

methods.label: Test common sandwich counts
methods.explanation:
Every sandwich uses the same number of globs and blobs. Therefore the total peanut butter glob count and the total jam blob count must both be divisible by the sandwich count \(N>1\).

If a proposed jam cost is \(c\) cents, the two total ingredient counts are
\[
\frac{253-c}{4}\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{c}{5}.
\]
For choices (A) through (E), respectively, these ordered pairs are
\[
(37,21),\ (32,25),\ (27,29),\ (22,33),\ (17,37).
\]
Their greatest common factors are, respectively,
\[
1,\ 1,\ 1,\ 11,\ 1.
\]
Thus only choice (D) permits a common sandwich count greater than \(1\).

It also works: take \(N=11\), giving \(22/11=2\) peanut butter globs and \(33/11=3\) jam blobs per sandwich. The total cost is \(11(4\cdot2+5\cdot3)=253\) cents. Hence the jam costs \(\boxed{\$1.65}\), choice (D).
methods.levelReason: This alternative uses elementary total-cost calculations and greatest common factors to inspect all five choices.
